newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM under fire for "stubborn" race stance.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM under fire for "stubborn" race stance.

text.p: Australia's rumbling race row has shown up a major failing in Australian Prime Minister John Howard -- people who know him say he can be too principled, even stubborn, for his own good.

Howard has repeatedly refused to openly condemn Pauline Hanson, the maverick MP whose anti-Asian comments started the national debate on race and immigration that has consumed Australia for almost two months.
His reasoning has been consistent: prime ministers should not have to step in every time a backbench politician says something controversial or offensive.

But as the row has gathered steam, Howard's refusal to get involved has opened him up to increasing criticism, both at home and in Asia, where his silence has been taken to imply support for Hanson's politics.
"The authority of Mr Howard's leadership is now hopelessly tangled with the nasty politics of racial intolerance," wrote Geoff Kitney of the The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper.
Gerard Henderson, a Howard chief of staff in the mid-1980s, agrees that Howard has mishandled the situation.

"I think the problem is that John Howard does not understand at times you have to send a totally unambiguous message. You can't hope that people are going to read all the nuances," Henderson, who heads the right-wing Sydney Institute think tank, told Reuters.
"I think he has a lot of ability...its just that he is quite stubborn and on some issues...he misreads the situation.
"It doesn't surprise me having got into this. He is not going to budge -- that is very much how he handles things."

This is not the first time Howard has felt the heat over race and immigration. He made well-publicised comments against Asian immigration in 1988 and the remarks still resonate in Asia despite his repudiation of them.

Asia has an historic suspicion of Australia when it comes to the issue of racism because of the now-defunct White Australia immigration policy which discriminated in favour of white migrants by using an English language dictation test.
In the past decade Asia's fears have been allayed as Australia's former Labor government pushed headlong into Asia, seeking a economic lifeline to the region's booming economies.
But Howard, who brought his conservative government to power in March, and his immediate predecessor, Labor's Paul Keating, are starkly different leaders.

Keating, a classical music aficionado and collector of antique French clocks, painted a grand vision of Australian integration into Asia. Howard, a stolid, straightforward man from middle-class, protestant Australia, is more concerned with his own backyard.

"Press the 'family' button to explain Howard, personally and politically," wrote Michelle Grattan, one of Australia's most influential political reporters, in a recent Howard profile in the Australian Financial Review Magazine.

These character differences, and Howard's 1988 comments that Asian immigration should be temporarily halted to help tackle high unemployment, are now fuelling concerns in Asia that Australia may be turning back the clock.
Asian newspaper editorials have called on Howard to clarify his position. "Howard's silence endorses Australia's racist fringe," said a headline in Bangkok's The Nation newspaper.

Henderson agrees that Howard's failure to condem Hanson last month, preferring to ignore her in the hope she and her views would disappear from the political landscape, was a serious error in leadership and reflects his softer style of politics.
Howard's three predecessors -- Keating, Labor's Bob Hawke and former Liberal prime minister Malcolm Fraser -- would have stamped out the debate before it even started, he believes.
And Henderson thinks that, even if its damaging his reputation, Howard will stick to his guns: "It is most unlikely he will change, he is very stubborn."
